title: Exponential-in-$N_c^2$ cost reduction of product-formula-based quantum simulations of quantum chromodynamics
abstract: Quantum algorithms for simulating quantum chromodynamics (QCD) have matured steadily since the pioneering work of Byrnes and Yamamoto [PRA 73, 022328 (2006)]. The most popular strategies for Hamiltonian simulation involve product-formula decompositions. However, the application of product-formula methods to SU($N_c$) lattice gauge theories by Byrnes and Yamamoto leads to $O(Λ^{8(N_c^2-1)})$ gate complexity per Trotter step, where $Λ$ is the bosonic cutoff in the electric (i.e., irreducible-representation) basis. A seminal work by Kan and Nam [arXiv:2107.12769 (2021)] significantly improves over such an undesirable cost and reports an $O\big(Λ\text{polylog}(Λ)\big)$ scaling, yet it still calls for an unrealistically large number of quantum gates. Here, we illuminate one of the reasons behind this high cost estimate and show that a factor of size $O(2^{4(N_c^2-1)})$ can be removed from the per-Trotter-step cost estimate by Kan and Nam. We specifically show that, by using methods developed in our past works [PRD 112, 014508 (2025); Quantum 7, 1213 (2023)], exponentiated-Hamiltonian decomposition---a necessary step in the application of product-formula algorithms---can be performed far more efficiently than previously thought. Our method reduces the T-gate cost estimate of QCD simulations using a second-order product formula by a factor of nearly $10^{14}$, independent of simulation parameters and sizes. Focusing on simulations in the electric basis, we further contrast our results with other methods: the local-multiplet basis approach of Ciavarella, Klco, and Savage [PRD 103, 094501 (2021)] and the near-optimal algorithm of Rhodes, Kreshchuk, and Pathak [PRX Quantum 5, 040347 (2024)]. This work highlights the importance of continued algorithmic improvement to bringing the quantum-simulation cost of QCD within reach of realistic quantum computers.
summary: This paper tackles the immense computational challenge of simulating Quantum Chromodynamics (QCD) on quantum computers using product-formula quantum algorithms. The authors introduce a novel, highly efficient method for decomposing the Hamiltonian, achieving an exponential cost reduction factor of $10^{14}$ compared to prior state-of-the-art estimates. This work is crucial for determining the feasibility of simulating fundamental particle physics models on near-term quantum hardware.
main_problem: Developing quantum algorithms capable of simulating the real-time dynamics of Quantum Chromodynamics (QCD) efficiently.
main_result: The authors demonstrate a method that reduces the T-gate cost estimate for QCD simulations using a second-order product formula by a factor of nearly $10^{14}$.
method: The core method involves performing an efficient exponentiated-Hamiltonian decomposition, which significantly improves upon previous product-formula-based Trotterization techniques.
model_or_system: The system is based on lattice gauge theories, specifically QCD with SU($N_c$) gauge groups, simulated via Hamiltonian evolution on a quantum computer.
key_observables: The primary focus is on the computational cost (T-gate count) required to simulate the time evolution operator $e^{-iT H}$.
important_parameters: The complexity scales with the number of colors ($N_c$) and the bosonic cutoff ($\Lambda$).
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on the product-formula decomposition of the time evolution operator and assumes the feasibility of implementing the derived Hamiltonian decompositions.
paper_structure: The paper reviews the problem of QCD simulation, details the limitations of previous product-formula methods (like Kan and Nam's), and then introduces and analyzes the new, highly efficient exponentiated-Hamiltonian decomposition technique.
why_interesting: While focused on QCD, the techniques developed for Hamiltonian decomposition and resource scaling are fundamental to simulating any complex, interacting quantum many-body system, which is relevant to AMO physics.

figures.caption: FIG. 1. A schematic representation of the nonzero electric- basis matrix elements of the U(1) plaquette Hamiltonian, Hplaq = UpUqU † s U † t + H.c., based on a 4D grid. Each point represents a basis state with quantum numbers (ϵp, ϵq, ϵs, ϵt). ϵp and ϵq (ϵs and ϵt) are the coordinates along the coarse outer (fine inner) axes. Each edge represents a mixing between two states by Hplaq, which generates moves of ±(1, 1, −1, −1) in the grid. In this example, a truncation ϵi ∈{0, ±1} is in effect, hence three blocks of points along the outer axes and three points within each block along the inner axes.

FIG. 2. Colorings of a graph representing the truncated U(1) plaquette Hamiltonian, Hplaq. In this example, each ϵi is truncated to four possible values to keep the drawing simple. The interpretation of the coordinates and edges is the same as in Fig. 1. (a) A coloring of the graph using two colors, corresponding to the two subevolutions by H(e) plaq and H(o) plaq. (b) A coloring of the graph using 24 = 16 colors, corresponding to the 16 subevolutions called for by the method of Ref. [22].
